title: Electromagnetic waves: how electric and magnetic fields carry energy
examples: How do electromagnetic waves travel through empty space?
What is the wavelength of 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi?
How much energy does sunlight carry?

figure.name: x-wave
figure.note: E and B at right angles, rising and falling together

explain.say: In 1887 Heinrich Hertz made sparks jump across a gap in one loop of wire and saw tiny sparks answer in another loop across the room. He had sent and caught radio waves, proving Maxwell right. On the board is an electromagnetic wave: an electric field and a magnetic field, waving together as they travel.

draw.text: Electromagnetic waves: how electric and magnetic fields carry energy

draw.name: x-wave
draw.note: E and B at right angles, rising and falling together

explain.say: Look closely. The electric field swings up and down, the magnetic field swings side to side at right angles to it, and both are at right angles to the direction of travel. They rise and fall in step, and each one's change creates the other, so the wave carries itself through empty space, needing no material at all. How fast does it go in a vacuum?

draw.name: x-wave
draw.note: E and B at right angles, rising and falling together

draw.text: E is at right angles to B, and both to the direction of travel.

explain.say: 300 million metres per second, the speed of light, c. Wavelength and frequency are tied together by c equals f times lambda. Your home Wi-Fi at 2.4 gigahertz has a wavelength of 3 times 10 to the 8, over 2.4 times 10 to the 9, which is 12.5 centimetres. What is the wavelength of FM radio at 100 megahertz?

draw.name: x-wave
draw.note: E and B at right angles, rising and falling together

explain.say: 3 metres. Here they are compared: FM radio 3 metres, mobile phones at 900 megahertz about 33 centimetres, Wi-Fi 12.5 centimetres, and 5G at 3.5 gigahertz under 9 centimetres. Higher frequency means a shorter wave, which is one reason phone antennas shrank as frequencies rose. Which of these has the shortest wavelength?

explain.say: 5G. Last, energy. The wave carries power across space, given by the Poynting vector, E times B over mu nought, in watts per square metre. Sunlight at the ground brings about 1000 watts per square metre, which means an electric field swinging by roughly 870 volts per metre. Superb! Challenge: what is the wavelength of 5 gigahertz Wi-Fi?

faq.a: A travelling disturbance of linked electric and magnetic fields. A changing electric field makes a magnetic field and the other way round, so the wave sustains itself, even in a vacuum.
asks: What is an EM wave made of?

faq.q: How do you find the wavelength of a radio wave?
faq.a: Divide the speed of light, 3 times 10 to the 8 metres per second, by the frequency. 100 megahertz FM radio has a wavelength of 3 metres.

faq.q: Why are E and B at right angles?
faq.a: Maxwell's equations require it: a changing field produces the other field circling around it, perpendicular to it, and both are perpendicular to the direction the wave travels.
asks: Why is the magnetic field perpendicular to the electric field?

faq.a: It gives the power per square metre carried by an electromagnetic wave, and its direction: E cross B over mu nought, in watts per square metre.
asks: How much energy does an EM wave carry?

faq.q: Why do higher frequencies need smaller antennas?
faq.a: Antennas work best at a size comparable to the wavelength, often a half or a quarter of it. A higher frequency means shorter waves, so smaller antennas.

facts: Heinrich Hertz first generated and detected radio waves in his laboratory in 1887.
All electromagnetic waves travel through a vacuum at about 299,792 kilometres per second.
